content.title: About
content.content: Basil is an aromatic annual herb from the Lamiaceae family. Fresh leaves are bright green, highly fragrant, and have a mildly peppery flavor. Basil is widely used in cooking, cosmetics, and traditional medicine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Basil originates from tropical and subtropical regions of Asia but is now cultivated worldwide.
There are more than 60 varieties, including Genovese, Thai, and Lemon basil.
In ancient Roman mythology basil was a symbol of love and prosperity.
Basil seeds are used as a spice and in aromatherapy.
Basil wilts quickly after harvest, so it is usually consumed fresh.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Leaves contain essential oils, flavonoids, and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Compounds such as eugenol and carvacrol stimulate bile production and aid digestion.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Basil exhibits moderate anti‑inflammatory effects that can be helpful during colds.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Fresh basil is virtually calorie‑free, making it a great addition to weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to basil, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Because of its high vitamin K content, basil may enhance the effects of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Fresh leaves can be contaminated with pesticides or bacteria, so they should be washed thoroughly before use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use fresh basil in salads, sauces (pesto), soups, marinades, and as a garnish. Leaves can be sliced, blended, or added whole to hot dishes at the end of cooking to preserve their aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh basil in the refrigerator in a sealed container with a damp paper towel for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze the leaves or make pesto and freeze in portioned bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Flank steak is a cut of beef taken from the abdominal muscles (the flank). It has a pronounced beefy flavor, moderate fat, and a fibrous texture. It is ideal for quick searing, marinating, and grilling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flank steak is considered a more "budget" cut, but when cooked properly it delivers great taste.
It is traditionally used in Mexican cuisine for fajitas.
The meat is rich in collagen, making it especially tender when slow‑braised.
In the United States the term "London broil" often refers to the cooking method rather than the specific cut.
Marinating flank in lime, garlic and spices enhances its flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Rich in creatine and carnitine
items.content: These compounds aid energy metabolism in muscles.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may contribute to elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogens such as E. coli.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels can aggravate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marinate flank steak for 2–4 hours, then sear quickly over high heat to medium‑rare and let rest 5–10 minutes. It can also be sliced thinly across the grain for fajitas or braised in a sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh flank steak in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Bulgur is a pre‑cooked, dried and cracked wheat of hard varieties. In this version a plant fat is added, which raises its energy value and gives a richer taste. The product is commonly used in Middle Eastern dishes, salads, side dishes and vegetarian patties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bulgur retains most of the nutrients of whole wheat, including fiber and B‑vitamins.
The added fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as vitamin E and carotenoids.
Bulgur cooks quickly: just pour hot water over it and let it stand for 10–15 minutes.
In traditional Middle Eastern cuisine bulgur is often served as couscous or tabbouleh.
Dry bulgur can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry place.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy, making bulgur a good choice for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: Contains plant fats
items.content: Added plant fats supply essential fatty acids and aid the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bulgur is rich in thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides magnesium, iron and phosphorus, important for bones, muscles and blood formation.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy should avoid bulgur.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat increases the product’s calories, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Bulgur contains small amounts of oxalates, which may be a concern for individuals prone to kidney stones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fat‑added bulgur can be used in salads (tabbouleh), as a side dish for meat or fish, in vegetable casseroles, vegetarian patties and soups. Typically it is poured over with hot water or broth and left to absorb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bulgur in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and light. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator or freezer.

chow-fun-noodles-with-meat-and-vegetable.title: Chow Fun Noodles with Meat and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Chow fun is a wide rice noodle traditionally used in Southern Chinese cuisine. This version is stir‑fried with strips of beef, fresh vegetables (carrot, bell pepper, onion) and a savory soy‑based sauce. The dish cooks quickly, offering a tender flavor and pleasant chew.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow fun means “wide rice noodle” and is a staple in dishes like Cantonese beef chow fun and street‑food stir‑fries.
Traditionally the noodles are steamed before being dried for long‑term storage, but modern production often uses extrusion and drying.
In the original recipe the protein can be swapped for seafood such as shrimp or squid.
The dish is commonly served in a wok to retain the high‑heat sear and smoky aroma.
In China chow fun is considered a comfort food, frequently prepared at home for quick meals.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice noodles provide sustained energy and help maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef adds complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, the dish contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for cholesterol‑controlled diets.

items.title: Glucosamine and chondroitin
items.content: Beef contains compounds that may support joint health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: While rice noodles are gluten‑free, soy sauce may contain wheat‑based gluten.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and seasonings can raise sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs)
items.content: High‑heat stir‑frying can generate PAHs; using moderate heat reduces this risk.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Undercooked or low‑quality beef can harbor bacteria, so use reputable sources and cook thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chow fun hot in a deep bowl. Garnish with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, or sliced chili for extra flavor. It works well as a main course or a quick lunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry noodles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked leftovers should be cooled quickly and refrigerated, lasting up to 2 days. Reheat in a wok or microwave with a splash of water to prevent drying out.

crackers-whole-grain-sandwich-peanut-but.title: Whole Grain Sandwich Crackers with Peanut Butter Filling

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain sandwich crackers with peanut butter filling are crunchy biscuits made from whole wheat grains and layered with a smooth peanut butter spread. They are convenient for a quick snack, lunchbox, or as part of a sandwich.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The crackers are made from whole grains, preserving more fiber and nutrients than refined snacks.
The peanut butter filling is produced without trans‑fats or artificial flavors.
These crackers are popular in school meals because of their handy size and kid‑friendly taste.
Each package typically contains 6–8 servings, making calorie control easy.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grain crackers provide soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: The peanut butter filling supplies about 8 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Peanut butter is high in monounsaturated fats, which can favorably affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains deliver thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Magnesium, phosphorus and iron are present, supporting muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Because the product contains peanut butter, it may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with peanut allergy.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The fat content of the filling makes the crackers relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties add salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the crackers straight from the pack, use them as a base for mini sandwiches, add them to salads, or pair with fresh fruit. For a softer texture, warm briefly in the oven.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For extended shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain crispness and prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels filled with a mixture of cheese and spinach. This version is served without sauce, allowing the delicate dough and aromatic filling to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional ravioli originate from Italy and have been made for over a thousand years.
The cheese‑and‑spinach combination provides a good balance of protein and vitamins.
Without sauce, ravioli are often finished with olive oil, fresh herbs, or grated Parmesan.
Spinach retains most of its nutrients thanks to the short cooking time.
A sauce‑free version is convenient for those watching calories and sugar intake.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cheese and spinach together supply a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese provides a substantial amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Spinach contains vitamin B6 and folate, which aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Leafy spinach is rich in lutein and vitamin C, helping protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: The absence of sauce makes the dish lower in calories and with a low glycemic impact.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to milk proteins.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Added sodium
items.content: Prepared ravioli sometimes contain added salt for flavor; those monitoring sodium should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil the ravioli in salted water for 3–4 minutes until al dente. Toss with a drizzle of olive oil, sprinkle with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs. They can also be added to salads or used as a base for a baked casserole.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry ravioli in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked ravioli store in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato and meat soup is a classic Russian dish consisting of a rich broth with tender pieces of boiled potato and chunks of beef or pork. It offers a hearty flavor, aromatic spices, and a comforting texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soup is often prepared in colder months as a warming meal.
Various types of meat can be used – beef, pork, chicken, or even lamb.
Traditional recipes include carrots, onion, and bay leaf for a distinctive aroma.
During the Soviet era, this soup was a staple in school cafeterias as a complete lunch.
Regional variations exist, such as adding pepper or tomato paste.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables deliver vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Bone‑based broth is rich in collagen and minerals that help strengthen immunity.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A hot broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The soup is often seasoned heavily; people with hypertension should monitor salt levels.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Using fatty cuts can make the dish calorie‑dense and high in saturated fat.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to certain types of meat.

items.title: Storage contamination
items.content: Leftover soup must be cooled quickly and refrigerated to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill and accompanied by crusty bread. A dollop of sour cream can add creaminess. Additional vegetables like celery, cabbage, or beans may be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, portion into freezer‑safe containers and freeze for 2‑3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.
